Gītagovinda
musical poem on the love of Kṛṣṇa an. Rādhā, intended for dance an. gesticulation, with recitative link verses; in 12 cantos comprising 24 dance-songs; a. each song is in eight feet, the poem is commonly called Aṣṭapadī, especially in South India; characterised variously a. ‘a little pastoral drama’ by Jones, ‘a lyric drama’ by Lassen, ‘a refined Yātrā’ by von Schroeder; an. a. being between song an. drama by Pischel an. Sylvain Levi. Pischel's view that the work goes back to a. original in Apabhram3śa (Die Hofdichter des Lakṣmaṇasena, p. 22) is not correct. (See Keith, History of Skt. Lit. p. 197 also Skt. Drama, p.. 17, 40, 272.). By Jayadeva, son of Bhojadeva an. Rāmādevī (Vāmādevī or Rādhādevī), of Keindubilva village (modern Kenduli) on the Ajay river in Birbhum district in West Bengal; there is also a strong tradition identifying J.'s birthplace a. being in Orissa; patronised by King Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal (
-1205); wife Padmāvatī is ref. to by a. a. a. accomplished danseuse (

, p.. 163-69; S. K. Chatterji, Acharya Dhruva Comm. Volume, p.. 183-199; Keith His.. of Skt. Lit. p.. 190-98; Wint. [Page026-b] HIL. Vol. III. Pt. I (Eng. transl.) p.. 142-48; S. K. D., History of Skt. Lit. p.. 392 ff; Presidency College Magazine, Calcutta, XVII. ii. 119 ff.; V. W. Karambelkar, IHQ. XXV. p.. 95-101. Endlessly imitated; forms the basis of the music an. dance traditions of South India. On its music see C. of Kumbhakarṇa; Rāgavibodha of Somanātha; Śg. II. p.. 59-63; J. of the Music Academy, Madras, XXXVI. p.. 176-182. On its Abhinaya see below under C. Abhinayaṭīkā an. the Malayalam work Aṣṭapadī-Āṭṭaprakāram, Kerala Uni. Mal.
